rosh_hashanah-6a-16-16.note: Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Papeyyas testified that the offspring of an animal set aside as a peace-offering must itself be sacrificed as a peace-offering. Rabbi Papeyyas gave a case from his own family: they had a cow that was a peace-offering and ate it on Passover, and they ate its calf as a peace-offering on the Festival.
rosh_hashanah-6a-16-16.why: Rava has just said that a person who lets even one Festival pass without bringing an offering he owes breaks a positive commandment. Rabbi Papeyyas's family seems to have waited past Shavuot, so the Gemara raises his account as an objection to Rava.

people.name: Rabbi Papeyyas
people.about: A Sage who testifies about what his family did with a peace-offering cow and its calf.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: A Sage who testifies together with Rabbi Papeyyas about the law.

terms.meaning: An animal sacrifice brought to the Temple. Most of its meat was eaten by the owners at a festive meal.
Here the translation takes it to mean Sukkot, the autumn festival. The Gemara later discusses whether it could mean Shavuot.
Gave formal evidence before the Sages about what the law is, based on a tradition or on events the speaker saw.

rosh_hashanah-14a-10-10.note: Rabbi Akiva picked an etrog on the first of Shevat and set aside two different tithes from it, one following Beit Shammai and one following Beit Hillel, because their rulings put that day in different tithe years. Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda disagrees about why he did it: he says Rabbi Akiva was not following Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel but the conflicting practices of Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Eliezer.
rosh_hashanah-14a-10-10.why: The mishna has just given the first of Shevat as the new year for trees, according to Beit Shammai. Rabbi Akiva's double tithe shows a Sage caught between the two dates. The Gemara then asks whether he was allowed to follow two opposing rulings at once.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A Sage who picks an etrog and sets aside two tithes from it because he is unsure of the law.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who gives a different reason for Rabbi Akiva's two tithes.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: A Sage whose ruling on how an etrog is tithed is one of the two Rabbi Akiva follows, according to Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: A Sage whose ruling on how an etrog is tithed is the other one, according to Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda.

terms.meaning: A citron, a citrus fruit used in the rituals of the Sukkot festival.
Portions of produce that had to be set aside by law. Which tithe was due depended on the year of the seven-year cycle the fruit belonged to.
The schools of two early Sages, Shammai and Hillel, who disagreed on many points of law. Here they disagree over whether the new year for trees falls on the first or the fifteenth of Shevat.
A winter month in the Hebrew calendar.

rosh_hashanah-17a-14-14.note: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, fell ill, and Rav Pappa came to visit him. Seeing that he was dying, Rav Pappa told those present to prepare his shrouds. In the end Rav Huna recovered, and Rav Pappa was embarrassed to see him. When asked what he had seen, Rav Huna said he really had been close to death. But the Holy One told the heavenly court that since Rav Huna did not insist on his rights against others, they should not be strict with him either.
rosh_hashanah-17a-14-14.why: Rava has just taught, from the verse 'He bears sin and forgives transgression,' that God forgives the sins of a person who lets go of the wrongs others did him. Rav Huna's recovery is told as an example, and he quotes the same verse.

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: A Sage who comes close to death and recovers. He tells what was decided about him in Heaven.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: A Sage who visits Rav Huna, has his shrouds prepared, and is later embarrassed when he recovers.

people.name: The Holy One, Blessed be He
people.about: God, who tells the heavenly court to be lenient with Rav Huna.

terms.meaning: A polite word for burial shrouds, the cloth in which the dead are wrapped.

terms.term: Does not stand on his rights
terms.meaning: Lets go of what others owe him and does not insist on getting back at people who wronged him.

rosh_hashanah-18a-7-7.note: Rava says the sin of Eli's house cannot be atoned for with sacrifices but can be atoned for through Torah study. Abaye says it can be atoned for through Torah study together with acts of kindness. The Gemara then reports that Rabba and Abaye were both descended from the house of Eli. Rabba, who studied Torah, lived forty years; Abaye, who studied Torah and did acts of kindness, lived sixty.
rosh_hashanah-18a-7-7.why: Rabbi Yonatan has just taught, from God's oath against the house of Eli, that a sentence sealed with an oath cannot be cancelled. Rava and Abaye limit that oath to sacrifices, and the lives of Rabba and Abaye are given as evidence for their view.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who says Torah study can atone for the sin of Eli's house.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage descended from the house of Eli. He studied Torah and did acts of kindness, and lived sixty years.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: A Sage descended from the house of Eli. He studied Torah and lived forty years.

terms.meaning: The family of Eli, a priest in the Bible. God swore that their sin would never be atoned for with sacrifice or offering.
Good deeds done for other people, such as helping, visiting or supporting them.

rosh_hashanah-18a-8-8.note: There was a family in Jerusalem whose members kept dying at eighteen. They came and told Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai. He said they might be descended from the family of Eli, of whom it is written that all the increase of the house would die young men. He told them to go and study Torah and they would live. They studied Torah and lived, and people called the family by Rabban Yohanan's name.
rosh_hashanah-18a-8-8.why: The Gemara has just said that the curse on the house of Eli cannot be atoned for with sacrifices but can be through Torah study. This baraita shows Torah study lifting that curse.

people.name: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai
people.about: The Sage the family turns to. He tells them to study Torah.

terms.meaning: A teaching from the early Sages that was left out of the Mishna, the first written code of Jewish law, but is quoted in the Gemara.
The descendants of Eli, a priest in the Bible. Scripture says that its members would die young.

rosh_hashanah-18b-11-11.note: Once the Sages decreed a fast on Hanukkah in the town of Lod. Rabbi Eliezer went down and bathed, and Rabbi Yehoshua went down and had his hair cut, to show they did not accept the fast. They told the others to go out and fast another fast to make up for the fast they had already kept.
rosh_hashanah-18b-11-11.why: Rav and Rabbi Hanina say the festive days listed in Megillat Ta'anit no longer apply. Rav Kahana raises this incident against them, since Hanukkah is one of those days and the Sages still would not allow a fast on it.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: A Sage who bathes on the fast day to show he rejects it.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: A Sage who has his hair cut on the fast day to show he rejects it.

terms.meaning: An ancient list of joyful days, commemorating good events, on which fasting and eulogies were forbidden.
Things a person refrains from on a public fast. Doing them showed that the Sages did not treat the day as a fast.

rosh_hashanah-19a-5-5.note: The wicked kingdom decreed that the Jews must not study Torah, must not circumcise their sons, and must desecrate Shabbat. Yehuda ben Shammua and his colleagues went for advice to a certain matron whom all the leading men of Rome visited. She told them to cry out at night. They went and cried out: O Heavens! Are we not your brothers, children of one father and one mother? How are we different from every other nation, that you issue harsh decrees against us? The decrees were annulled, and that day, the twenty-eighth of Adar, was made a festive day.
rosh_hashanah-19a-5-5.why: The Gemara is asking whether Megillat Ta'anit has been cancelled. Rav Tovi bar Mattana objects with this festive day, added after the Temple's destruction: no one adds days to a list that was cancelled.

people.name: Yehuda ben Shammua
people.about: Leads his colleagues to seek advice and cry out against the decree

people.name: Rav Tovi bar Mattana
people.about: Cites this festive day in the Gemara's debate

terms.meaning: An ancient list of days of rejoicing on which fasting is forbidden.
A noble Roman lady.
The text's name for the hostile ruling power, here Rome.

rosh_hashanah-21a-1-1.note: Levi arrived in Babylonia on the day the people there counted as the eleventh of Tishrei. He remarked how tasty the Babylonians' food was on the very day Yom Kippur was being kept in the Land of Israel, where the date was a day behind. The people asked him to testify, so that they could keep Yom Kippur that day. He refused, saying he had not himself heard the court declare the month sanctified.
rosh_hashanah-21a-1-1.why: The Gemara is discussing how Jews outside the Land of Israel kept festival days when they were unsure how the court there had fixed the month. Levi's visit shows the two communities on different days, and that a witness must have heard the court himself.

people.name: Levi
people.about: A Sage who travels from the Land of Israel to Babylonia and notices the calendar difference.

terms.meaning: The autumn month that begins with Rosh HaShana. Yom Kippur falls on its tenth day.
What the Babylonian Sages called the Land of Israel, which lay to their west.
The words the court in the Land of Israel said aloud when it officially declared a new month. That declaration fixed the date of the festivals.

rosh_hashanah-21a-3-3.note: Rabbi Aivu bar Naggarei and Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba came to a place that the messengers announcing the new month reached in Nisan but not in Tishrei. The people there kept only one day of Passover, and the two Sages said nothing. Rabbi Yohanan heard and was angry. He told them: 'Did I not tell you that wherever the Nisan messengers arrive but the Tishrei messengers do not, they must keep two days, a decree for Nisan because of Tishrei?'
rosh_hashanah-21a-3-3.why: The Gemara has just quoted Rabbi Yohanan's rule that such places must keep two days of Passover, so that they would not come to keep Sukkot for only one day. This story shows how seriously he took it.

people.name: Rabbi Aivu bar Naggarei
people.about: A student of Rabbi Yohanan who did not correct the local practice.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba
people.about: A student of Rabbi Yohanan who traveled with Rabbi Aivu and also kept silent.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Their teacher, who was angry that they did not enforce his ruling.

terms.meaning: Riders sent out from the court in the Land of Israel to tell distant communities which day the month had begun, so they would know when to keep the festivals.
The months of Passover (spring) and Sukkot (autumn). In Tishrei the messengers could not travel on Rosh HaShana and Yom Kippur, so they got less far.
A rule the Sages added to protect the law. Here, two days of Passover were required so that people would not come to keep Sukkot for only one day.

rosh_hashanah-21a-4-6.note: Rava used to fast two days for Yom Kippur, in case the month had begun a day later than people in Babylonia thought. Once it turned out he was right. Rav Nahman once fasted the whole of Yom Kippur. In the evening a man came and told him that the next day was Yom Kippur in the Land of Israel. Rav Nahman asked where he was from, and the man said Damihareya. Rav Nahman made a pun on the name, 'Blood will be his end,' and applied to him the verse 'Our pursuers were swifter.' The text does not say what he did the next day.
rosh_hashanah-21a-4-6.why: These reports follow Levi's discovery that Babylonia kept Yom Kippur a day before the Land of Israel. They show two Sages facing the same doubt about which day was really Yom Kippur.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who regularly fasted two days for Yom Kippur. Once his caution proved right.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: A Sage told at the end of his fast that Yom Kippur was actually the next day.

terms.meaning: A name for Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, a full day of fasting.
What the Babylonian Sages called the Land of Israel, which lay to their west.
The man's hometown. Rav Nahman makes a pun on it with the word for blood, because he faces a second day of fasting.

rosh_hashanah-22a-0-0.note: More than forty pairs of witnesses were on their way to Jerusalem to report seeing the new moon, and someone stopped them in Lod. The mishna says it was Rabbi Akiva. Rabbi Yehuda says, 'Heaven forbid that Rabbi Akiva stopped them'; it was Zefer, the head of the town of Geder. Rabban Gamliel sent for him, and Zefer was removed from his high office.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: The Sage the mishna says stopped the witnesses. Rabbi Yehuda denies it.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who says it was not Rabbi Akiva who stopped the witnesses.

people.name: Zefer
people.about: The head of the town of Geder. According to Rabbi Yehuda, he stopped the witnesses and lost his office for it.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The head of the court, who had Zefer removed from office.

terms.meaning: People who saw the first sliver of the new moon and went to the court in Jerusalem to report it, so that the court could declare the new month.
The first written code of Jewish law. The Gemara is a discussion of the mishna, explaining and debating it line by line.

rosh_hashanah-22b-6-9.note: The Boethusians tried to mislead the Sages about the new moon. They paid two men four hundred dinars to give false testimony: one of their own, and one of the Sages' people. Their man testified and left. The Sages' man was asked to describe the moon, and described it like an animal crouching between rocks, with a calf's head and a deer's horns. He said he had looked, got scared and fallen backward, and that the two hundred dinars he was paid were in his cloak. He said he had done it to warn the Sages. They let him keep the money and ruled that the man who hired him be flogged. From then on they accepted testimony only from witnesses they knew.
rosh_hashanah-22b-6-9.why: The mishna says that at first the court accepted testimony about the new moon from anyone. The Gemara quotes this baraita to show what went wrong and why that changed.

terms.meaning: A Jewish sect that opposed the Sages and disagreed with them about the calendar.
The court declared a new month only after witnesses came and said they had seen the new moon. False witnesses could therefore shift the dates of the festivals.
Silver coins.
Tied to a post to be flogged.

rosh_hashanah-25a-9-10.note: Once the sky was covered with clouds, and something that looked like the moon was seen on the twenty-ninth of the month. The people thought it was the New Moon, and the court wanted to declare it. Rabban Gamliel told them that he had a tradition from his grandfather's house: the moon's cycle is never shorter than twenty-nine and a half days plus a little more. That same day the mother of ben Zaza died. Rabban Gamliel gave her a great eulogy, not because she deserved it, but so the people would know the court had not declared the New Moon.
rosh_hashanah-25a-9-10.why: The Gemara has just quoted Rabban Gamliel's family tradition that the moon's path is sometimes long and sometimes short. This baraita shows him using that same tradition to stop the court from declaring the month too early.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The head of the court, who stops the New Moon from being declared too early and uses a eulogy to make the point public.

people.name: Ben Zaza
people.about: A Sage whose mother died that day.

terms.meaning: The first day of a Hebrew month, which the court declared once it accepted that the new moon had been seen. It is a minor festival.
A public speech mourning someone who has died. Eulogies are not allowed on the New Moon, so giving one showed the day was not the New Moon.

rosh_hashanah-25a-11-11.note: The head of the court had ordered Rabbi Yehoshua to break the day he believed was Yom Kippur. Rabbi Akiva found him distressed and asked why. Rabbi Yehoshua said it would be better to lie sick in bed for twelve months than to have such a decree laid on him. Rabbi Akiva asked to remind him of something Rabbi Yehoshua himself had taught. The Torah says three times that the festivals are what 'you' proclaim, which teaches that the court's date stands even if it errs by accident, on purpose, or because it was misled. Rabbi Yehoshua answered: 'Akiva, you have consoled me, you have consoled me.'
rosh_hashanah-25a-11-11.why: The mishna says Rabbi Akiva found 'him' distressed, and the Gemara asks which Sage was upset. It cites this baraita to show it was Rabbi Yehoshua, comforted by the rule that the court's date for the month stands.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A Sage who finds his teacher distressed and comforts him with his teacher's own teaching.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: Rabbi Akiva's teacher, upset at being ordered to break the day he held was Yom Kippur.

terms.meaning: Two Hebrew words that are spelled almost alike. Otam means 'them' and atem means 'you'. Reading 'them' as 'you' teaches that the court has the power to set the dates of the festivals.
The Day of Atonement, a full day of fasting. Its date depends on when the court declared the month had begun.

rosh_hashanah-25b-3-3.note: Rabbi Yehoshua had disagreed with Rabban Gamliel, the head of the court, over which day was Yom Kippur. Ordered to appear on the day his own reckoning made Yom Kippur, he came carrying his staff and his money. When Rabban Gamliel saw him, he rose from his chair, kissed him on the head, and greeted him as 'my teacher and my student': teacher because he had taught Torah in public, student because he obeyed Rabban Gamliel's decree. He added: fortunate is the generation in which the greater heed the lesser.
rosh_hashanah-25b-3-3.why: The Gemara has just taught that whoever is appointed leader of his generation must be obeyed like the greatest of the great. Rabbi Yehoshua, the greater scholar, submitting to Rabban Gamliel's ruling is that teaching in action.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: A Sage who disputed Rabban Gamliel's calendar; Rabban Gamliel calls him his teacher, since he taught Torah in public.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Head of the court, who ordered Rabbi Yehoshua to appear and then received him with honor.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.
An argument from the stronger case to the weaker: if something holds in a less likely case, it surely holds in a more likely one.
The Day of Atonement, a fast day on which carrying a staff and money is forbidden. Coming with them on that date meant treating it as an ordinary weekday.

rosh_hashanah-26a-20-20.note: The Sage Levi came to a certain place, and a man complained to him: 'So-and-so keva'a from me.' Levi did not know the word, so he went and asked in the study hall, where he was told it means 'robbed', as in the verse 'Will a man rob God?' Later, Rava from Barnish told Rav Ashi that had he been there, he would simply have asked the man how, with what and why he was keva'a, and worked out the meaning himself. The Gemara explains that Levi thought the man was raising a question of prohibition, where such questions would not have helped.
rosh_hashanah-26a-20-20.why: The Gemara is collecting cases in which the Sages learned the meaning of a rare word in Scripture from how ordinary people spoke in particular places. This one explains the verb in Malachi 3:8.

people.name: Levi
people.about: A Sage who visited a certain place and could not understand a man's complaint.

people.name: Rava from Barnish
people.about: A Sage who said how he would have worked out the word's meaning had he been in Levi's place.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: The Sage to whom Rava from Barnish made his remark.

terms.meaning: The house of study where Sages gathered to learn and discuss Torah, and where a question like Levi's could be put to other scholars.

rosh_hashanah-26b-1-1.note: The Sages did not know what the word seirugin meant. One day they heard the maidservant in the house of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi call out to Sages who were coming into the house in small groups, one after another: 'How long will you come in seirugin seirugin?' From this they understood that the word means 'at intervals'.
rosh_hashanah-26b-1-1.why: This is one of a run of anecdotes in which the meaning of a puzzling word in the Mishna or Scripture is learned from everyday speech, here from the household of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.

people.name: the maidservant in Rabbi's house
people.about: A servant in the household of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi whose everyday speech taught the Sages several rare words.

terms.meaning: Used alone, the title refers to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, the Sage who compiled the Mishna.
A teaching from the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law, on which the Gemara comments.

rosh_hashanah-26b-2-2.note: The Sages did not know what the word haloglogot meant, though it appears in several early teachings. One day they heard the maidservant in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's house speak to a man she saw scattering his purslane plants: 'How long will you scatter your haloglogot?' So they learned that haloglogot means purslane.
rosh_hashanah-26b-2-2.why: Another in the Gemara's string of cases where an obscure word was explained by overhearing the maidservant in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's house.

people.name: the maidservant in Rabbi's house
people.about: A servant in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's household whose speech revealed the meaning of the word.

terms.meaning: A leafy plant, eaten as a vegetable, that grows low and spreads along the ground.
Teachings of the early Sages: those collected in the Mishna (mishnayot) and those left out of it (baraitot).

rosh_hashanah-26b-3-3.note: The Sages did not know what salseleha meant in the verse 'Salseleha and it will exalt you,' which speaks of wisdom. One day they heard the maidservant in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's house say to a man who was curling his hair: 'How long will you mesalsel your hair?' From this they understood the verse to mean: turn wisdom over and over, and it will exalt you.
rosh_hashanah-26b-3-3.why: Part of the Gemara's series of words in Scripture whose meaning the Sages learned from the maidservant in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's house.

people.name: the maidservant in Rabbi's house
people.about: A servant in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's household whose words explained the verse.

rosh_hashanah-26b-4-4.note: The Sages did not know the meaning of the words in Isaiah's verse 'And I will sweep it with the broom of destruction.' One day they heard the maidservant in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's house tell a fellow worker: 'Take a broom and sweep the house,' using the same words, and so they understood the verse.
rosh_hashanah-26b-4-4.why: Another in the Gemara's run of puzzling words in Scripture explained by overhearing the maidservant in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's house.

people.name: the maidservant in Rabbi's house
people.about: A servant in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's household; her instruction to a fellow worker explained the verse.

rosh_hashanah-26b-5-5.note: The Sages did not know what yehavkha meant in the verse 'Cast your yehavkha upon the Lord and He will sustain you.' Rabba bar bar Hana told how he was once traveling with an Arab while carrying a load, and the Arab said to him: 'Take your yehav and throw it on my camel.' From this he learned that yehav means a load.
rosh_hashanah-26b-5-5.why: The last of the Gemara's series of rare words explained from everyday speech; this time the source is not Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's maidservant but an Arab traveler.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: A Sage who learned the meaning of the word from a traveling companion.

people.name: the Arab
people.about: A traveler with a camel who offered to carry Rabba bar bar Hana's load.

rosh_hashanah-29b-11-12.note: Once Rosh Hashana fell on Shabbat, and people from all the towns gathered in Yavne. Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai said to the sons of Beteira: 'Let us sound the shofar.' They answered: 'Let us discuss it.' He told them: 'Let us sound it, and discuss it afterward.' Once the shofar had been sounded, they said: 'Now let us discuss it.' He replied: 'The horn has already been heard in Yavne, and one does not argue against a ruling after it has been acted on.'
rosh_hashanah-29b-11-12.why: The Gemara has just explained that the Sages forbade sounding the shofar on Shabbat, lest someone carry it in public. The mishna says that after the Temple's destruction Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai allowed it in Yavne; this account shows how that happened.

people.name: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai
people.about: The Sage who led the gathering at Yavne and had the shofar sounded on Shabbat.

people.name: the sons of Beteira
people.about: Leading legal authorities, who wanted to debate the question before the shofar was sounded.

terms.meaning: A ram's horn blown on Rosh Hashana, the Jewish New Year.
A town where the Sages' court sat after the Temple in Jerusalem was destroyed.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.

rosh_hashanah-31b-3-4.note: A woman was summoned to a lawsuit before Ameimar in Neharde'a. Ameimar then went to Mehoza for a time, and she did not follow him there, so he wrote a document of excommunication against her. Rav Ashi challenged him: the mishna says that witnesses go only to the court's usual meeting place, even if its head is elsewhere. Ameimar answered that this applies only to witnesses who report the new moon, who must not be discouraged from coming in future. In money cases, he said, 'the borrower is servant to the lender'.
rosh_hashanah-31b-3-4.why: The mishna has just stated Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai's rule that witnesses must go to the court's meeting place rather than follow its head. The Gemara uses this case to show the rule is limited to testimony about the new moon.

people.name: Ameimar
people.about: A judge in Neharde'a who excommunicated a woman for not following him to Mehoza.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: A Sage who challenged Ameimar's ruling by citing the mishna.

terms.meaning: A court order that put a person under a ban, cutting them off from the community, until they obeyed the court.
The court began each month on the word of witnesses who had seen the new moon, so it needed them to keep coming.
A teaching from the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law, on which the Gemara comments.

rosh_hashanah-31b-10-11.note: Rabbi Eliezer had a vineyard in its fourth year east of Lod, beside the village of Tavi, and he wanted to declare its fruit ownerless for the poor. His students told him: 'Our teacher, your colleagues have already voted on this and permitted it.' The Gemara explains that 'your colleagues' means Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai.
rosh_hashanah-31b-10-11.why: Rav Pappa holds that one of Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai's nine ordinances concerned fourth-year fruit grown near Jerusalem, which had to be carried there to fill its markets. This account is his evidence that the requirement was cancelled.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: Owner of a fourth-year vineyard near Lod, who wanted to give its fruit to the poor.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer's students
people.about: They told him his colleagues had already voted to permit the fruit.

people.name: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai
people.about: The Gemara says he is the 'colleagues' the students meant.

terms.meaning: Fruit from a vine's fourth year is holy and must be eaten in Jerusalem, or redeemed for money. Vines within a day's walk of Jerusalem had to bring the fruit itself.
Property given up by its owner so that anyone, here the poor, may take it.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.

rosh_hashanah-32a-12-12.note: When the court fixed the year's calendar in Usha, Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka led the Rosh Hashana prayer before Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, following Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri's order of the blessings. Rabban Shimon told him: 'That was not the custom in Yavne.' On the second day Rabbi Hanina, son of Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, led the prayer following Rabbi Akiva's order, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel said: 'This was the custom in Yavne.'
rosh_hashanah-32a-12-12.why: The Gemara is debating where in the Rosh Hashana prayer the blessings of Kingship and the holiness of the day belong. Afterward it asks how Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel could approve Rabbi Akiva's order, when he places these blessings differently himself.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka
people.about: Led the prayer at Usha in the order of Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri, and was told it was not the Yavne custom.

people.name: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
people.about: The Sage before whom the prayer was led, who judged each leader against the custom of Yavne.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina, son of Rabbi Yosei HaGelili
people.about: Led the prayer on the second day in the order of Rabbi Akiva.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri
people.about: A Sage whose order of the Rosh Hashana blessings the first prayer leader followed.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A Sage whose order of the blessings the second prayer leader followed.

terms.meaning: The court's act of fixing the calendar, deciding when months and the new year begin.
The leader of public prayer stood in front of the congregation, often at a lower place, so leading the prayer is called 'descending'.
One of the special blessings of the Rosh Hashana prayer, made up of verses that proclaim God as King.

rosh_hashanah-34b-3-3.note: Rabbi Abbahu was walking behind Rabbi Yohanan and reciting the Shema prayer. When he reached alleys that were filthy with excrement, where words of Torah may not be spoken, he fell silent. Once he had passed through, he asked Rabbi Yohanan whether he could go on from where he had stopped. Rabbi Yohanan told him: if you paused long enough to have said the whole of it, go back to the beginning.
rosh_hashanah-34b-3-3.why: The Gemara has ruled that, for Rabbi Yohanan, shofar blasts heard at different times of day still count, and has said his stricter rule about long pauses is his teacher's view. This story challenges that, since Rabbi Yohanan seems to rule strictly himself.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: A Sage walking behind Rabbi Yohanan, who broke off his Shema in a filthy alley.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: The Sage Rabbi Abbahu was following, who told him to start the Shema again.

terms.meaning: The central declaration of Jewish faith, 'Hear O Israel', recited every morning and evening.
